extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of Darwin; authors and peer-reviewers of scientific monographs (19th-century natural history context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and embedded evaluative principles for preparing, correcting, sending, and judging a scientific monograph (proofs, revisions, evidence balance, reviewer conduct) as revealed in Darwin's letters and Huxley's commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and smoothness of prose/style
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin repeatedly emphasizes that the style must be clear and smooth (he found his MS 'incredibly bad, and most difficult to make clear and smooth'; 'I have tried my best to make it clear and striking').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should heavily revise and rewrite proofs if necessary; expect heavy corrections and rewriting to achieve clarity. Darwin notes that lack of attention to details (focusing on the general argument instead) produced poor style. Aim for 'clear and striking' presentation; correct proofs even if corrections are 'very heavy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing difficulties and counterarguments fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin asks reviewers to judge whether 'I have given the difficulties fairly' and states that the last chapter 'sums up and balances in a mass all the arguments contra and pro'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong scholarly work should present objections and difficulties openly and balance pro and contra evidence rather than ignoring problems. Reviewers should check that difficulties are acknowledged and that the balance is fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple, converging lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin lists Geological Succession, Geographical Distribution, Morphology, Embryology and Rudimentary Organs as the parts that 'tell most in favour of the view'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective scientific argument should marshal diverse types of evidence (geology, distributional data, morphology, embryology, vestigial structures) to support a hypothesis; reviewers should evaluate the strength and integration of these lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer open-mindedness / avoid premature commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin implores: 'Do not, I beg, be in a hurry in committing yourself (like so many naturalists) to go a certain length and no further; for I am deeply convinced that it is absolutely necessary to go the whole vast length, or stick to the creation of each separate species.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should keep an open mind, avoid snap judgments, and consider the whole argument before deciding; do not prematurely accept only part of an approach or reject it without full consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actionable margin comments from reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin requests: 'When, and if, you reread, I supplicate you to write on the margin the word "expand," when too condensed, or "not clear." or "?".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should give concise, actionable margin annotations indicating where text needs expansion, clarification, or where they have questions; such marks are highly valuable to authors revising proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clean sheets, diagrams, indexes and revises to reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin offers to send 'clean sheets' and a diagram (for Chapter IV), notes that index and revises are parts of the finished work, and asks whether to send last perfect revises as he corrects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When soliciting peer comment, provide the clearest possible copy (clean sheets), include explanatory diagrams for complex arguments, and ensure ancillary materials (index, final revises) are available; these assist reviewers in judging and commenting effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence completeness vs. abstracts (provide full facts and authorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin warns readers that his book, as sent to some, is 'only an Abstract (but has cost me above thirteen months to write!!), and facts and authorities are far from given in full.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should understand that abstracts/summaries are insufficient for full evaluation; full works should provide complete facts, data, and authorities. Reviewers should take care to note when a work is an abstract and withhold full judgment until supporting details are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to rewrite substantially for future editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin states: 'My larger book will have to be wholly re-written, and not merely the present volume expanded; so that I want to waste as little time over this volume as possible, if another edition be called for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be open to major revision between editions; reviewers' detailed feedback can and should guide substantial rewriting rather than mere patching. Consider when a work needs comprehensive reworking rather than incremental edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibility and influence — read the whole argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin reminds Lyell: 'Remember that your verdict will probably have more influence than my book... I shall be most deeply delighted if you do come round, especially if I have a fair share in the conversion, I shall then feel that my career is run.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers wield substantial influence on reception; they have a responsibility to read the full work (including crucial later chapters and recapitulations) before issuing a verdict, and to weigh the whole argument carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagrams and illustrative figures to clarify perplexing chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin warns Chapter IV 'will be perplexing and unintelligible, without the aid of the enclosed queer diagram (The diagram illustrates descent with divergence.).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex conceptual arguments benefit from clear diagrams; include figures that directly aid comprehension and signal to reviewers/readers where visual aids are essential to understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate external commentators for dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin asks for addresses of 'good and SPECULATIVE foreigners to whom it would be worth while to send copies' and debates whom to send abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/publishers should choose reviewers/commentators with relevant perspectives (including speculative or international scholars) who can engage productively with the work; consider language ability and subject fit when sending copies abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and professional virtues of a credible scientist/author
rubrics_metrics.description: Huxley characterizes Darwin as combining 'genius, industry, and unswerving veracity', being 'ready to listen with patience and respect to the most insignificant of reasonable objectors', and 'kept himself clear of all envy, hatred, and malice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating scientific contributions, consider the author's intellectual honesty, industriousness, fairness in debate, willingness to engage with objections, and personal integrity as relevant contextual virtues that bolster trust in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the work accessible to its intended readership (avoid excessive perplexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin frets 'I begin to fear that the public will find it intolerably dry and perplexing' and repeatedly tries to make passages clearer and to mark where expansion is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should tailor exposition to the intended audience; make difficult parts as comprehensible as possible (with clearer prose, diagrams, or expansions) to avoid alienating readers beyond specialist circles.
